extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, legislators, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the principles, effects, and policy implications of the commercial (mercantile) system compared and contrasted with an agricultural system of political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Political economy, considered as a branch of the science of a statesman or legislator, proposes two distinct objects; first, to provide a plentiful revenue or subsistence for the people, or, more properly, to enable them to provide such a revenue or subsistence for themselves; and, secondly, to supply the state or commonwealth with a revenue sufficient for the public services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It proposes to enrich both the people and the sovereign; these two ends (private subsistence/self-sufficiency and public revenue) are the evaluative aims for systems of political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-system classification (commerce vs agriculture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The different progress of opulence in different ages and nations, has given occasion to two different systems of political economy, with regard to enriching the people. The one may be called the system of commerce, the other that of agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this dichotomy as a framework: explain and assess each system's principles, mechanisms, and consequences; the text starts with the system of commerce as the modern example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile principle: wealth consists in money
rubrics_metrics.description: That wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver, is a popular notion which naturally arises from the double function of money, as the instrument of commerce, and as the measure of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underpins mercantilist policy: money's role as medium of exchange and measure of value makes bullion accumulation appear the readiest way to enrich a country; examples and objections follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullion-accumulation policy (prohibit export of gold and silver)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the different nations of Europe have studied, though to little purpose, every possible means of accumulating gold and silver in their respective countries. Spain and Portugal ... have either prohibited their exportation under the severest penalties, or subjected it to a considerable duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical policy instruments include export prohibitions, duties, and statutes forbidding export of specie; these are cited as characteristic mercantilist responses to belief that wealth = bullion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locke's distinction: money vs consumable moveable goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr Locke remarks a distinction between money and other moveable goods. All other moveable goods ... are of so consumable a nature, that the wealth which consists in them cannot be much depended on; and a nation which abounds in them one year may ... be in great want of them the next. Money ... if it can be kept from going out of the country, is not very liable to be wasted and consumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reasoning is used to justify focusing on metals as the 'most solid and substantial' part of a nation's moveable wealth and to prioritize their accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantilist caveat for nations with foreign connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Others admit, that if a nation could be separated from all the world, it would be of no consequence how much or how little money circulated in it. ... But it is otherwise, they think, with countries which have connections with foreign nations, and which are obliged to carry on foreign wars, and to maintain fleets and armies in distant countries. This, they say, cannot be done, but by sending abroad money to pay them with; and a nation cannot send much money abroad, unless it has a good deal at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mercantilist rationale is strongest for powers engaged in foreign wars and maintaining distant fleets/armies; accumulation of bullion is seen as strategic capacity for such expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities provide markets that encourage rural improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To all of them [neighboring countries] they afforded a market for some part either of their rude or manufactured produce, and, consequently, gave some encouragement to the industry and improvement of all. Their own country, however, on account of its neighbourhood, necessarily derived the greatest benefit from this market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urban commerce creates proximate markets for rural produce; lower carriage costs let growers receive better prices and encourage agricultural improvement—an evaluative criterion for commerce's local benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchants as superior improvers of land
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants are commonly ambitious of becoming country gentlemen, and, when they do, they are generally the best of all improvers. A merchant is accustomed to employ his money chiefly in profitable projects; whereas a mere country gentleman is accustomed to employ it chiefly in expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess land improvement prospects by the character of the purchaser: merchants' habits of investment, order, and economy make them more likely to undertake profitable improvements than traditional country gentlemen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and manufactures introduce order, liberty, and security
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, and lastly, commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals, among the inhabitants of the country, who had before lived almost in a continual state of war with their neighbours, and of servile dependency upon their superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a criterion for evaluating economic change: the expansion of trade and manufacture is credited with reducing feudal violence and dependency, thereby supporting civil government and individual liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence produced when surplus consumed on the estate
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country which has neither foreign commerce nor any of the finer manufactures, a great proprietor ... consumes the whole in rustic hospitality. He is at all times, therefore, surrounded with a multitude of retainers and dependants, who, having no equivalent to give in return for their maintenance, but being fed entirely by his bounty, must obey him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social/political dependence and private jurisdiction stem from on-estate consumption of surplus; this explains strong local authority of great proprietors prior to commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feudal law limited compared with commercial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of the feudal law, so far from extending, may be regarded as an attempt to moderate, the authority of the great allodial lords. ... it could not alter sufficiently that state of property and manners from which the disorders arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal-institutional reforms like feudal subordination did not by themselves create order; the text argues commerce/manufactures achieved what feudal law could not, so evaluate reforms against the deeper property/manners causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real national capital must be realized in land or lasting improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital, however, that is acquired to any country by commerce and manufactures, is always a very precarious and uncertain possession, till some part of it has been secured and realized in the cultivation and improvement of its lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital held by merchants is mobile; only when invested in buildings or lasting land improvements can it be considered securely part of the country's durable capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primogeniture & perpetuities hinder multiplication of small proprietors
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe, the law of primogeniture, and perpetuities of different kinds, prevent the division of great estates, and thereby hinder the multiplication of small proprietors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal rules that keep land out of market maintain high prices and discourage small-capital investment in land; evaluate legal regimes by their impact on small-proprietor formation and agricultural improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy instruments claimed to favour agriculture (England example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in times of scarcity, the exportation of corn is not only free, but encouraged by a bounty. In times of moderate plenty, the importation of foreign corn is loaded with duties that amount to a prohibition. The importation of live cattle, except from Ireland, is prohibited at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are cited as direct legal/ fiscal encouragements for agriculture; the author notes they demonstrate legislative intent to favor agriculture even if their ultimate effect may be illusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth tied to agricultural-based wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the slow progress of those European countries of which the wealth depends very much upon their commerce and manufactures, with the rapid advances of our North American colonies, of which the wealth is founded altogether in agriculture. Through the greater part of Europe, the number of inhabitants is not supposed to double in less than five hundred years. In several of our North American colonies, it is found to double in twenty or five-and-twenty years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population growth rates as an evaluative metric for the systemic effects of an agricultural versus commercial economic basis; land availability and ease of starting plantations make agricultural economies expand faster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of long leases to encourage tenant improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: His tenants could agree to this upon one condition only, that they should be secured in their possession for such a term of years as might give them time to recover, with profit, whatever they should lay out in the further improvement of the land. ... Hence the origin of long leases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long leases are a policy/institutional response to incentivize tenant investment: evaluate tenancy arrangements by whether they give tenants time to recoup improvements and thus encourage land improvement.
